claims.text: The starting material is an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy containing hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries generate local stress concentrations in the untreated alloy.
The local stress concentrations caused by dislocation pile-ups promote microcracking and brittle damage.
An intermediate-temperature annealing treatment at approximately 600°C can selectively recrystallize the soft FCC lamellae adjacent to the hard phase.
The proposed treatment will produce semi-coherent interfaces between the selectively recrystallized soft phase and the retained hard phase.
Selective recrystallization softens the interfacial regions of the FCC lamellae.
Softened interfacial regions facilitate dislocation absorption at internal boundaries.
Selectively recrystallized interfaces facilitate smoother dislocation transmission across internal boundaries.
Improved dislocation absorption and transmission reduce dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations suppresses microcrack nucleation during tensile straining.
The annealing treatment can preserve the overall dual-phase lamellar framework.
The retained dual-phase lamellar framework is responsible for preserving high strength.
The treatment will significantly enhance room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will retain or moderately increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Over-annealing could cause complete homogenization and loss of the beneficial lamellar microstructural features.
Loss of the dual-phase lamellar architecture could compromise the ductility-strength balance.
